issues.legal_issue: An inam grant must be shown to cover the whole village to qualify as an estate under the main part of the statutory definition.
material_facts: The grant was described as covering a named village, but the recorded estimates of its area varied and did not establish that the entire village was included in the grant.
issues.conclusion: The suit lands were not shown to constitute a whole inam village under the main part of the definition, although they could still constitute an estate under the Explanation.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, the main part applies to an inam village; the court found that the evidence did not establish that the grant covered the whole village. The Explanation may nevertheless apply in the circumstances addressed in the separate issue concerning grants of named villages.

predicates.inam_estate_classification_case: A court is deciding whether land covered by an inam grant constitutes an estate.
predicates.grant_extent_not_shown_to_cover_whole_vi: The evidence about the grant's extent does not establish that it covered the entire village.

issues.definition: When a court classifies inam land and the grant's extent is not shown to cover the whole village, the land does not qualify under the main definition.

issues.legal_issue: A grant expressed to be of a named village does not by itself create a presumption that the land constitutes an estate when some lands within the village were separately granted.
material_facts: The grant confirmed by the principal title deed was expressed to be of a named village.
Other lands within the village were covered by minor inam grants, but the evidence did not establish when those grants were made.
issues.conclusion: The legislature created no presumption either that the land was, or that it was not, an estate. A named-village grant can fall within the Explanation where the excluded minor inams had been granted before the grant of the rest of the village as a named village; the named-village description alone does not establish that fact.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied Explanation (1) to section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, and approved Varadaraja-Swamivari Temple v. Krishnappa. It rejected the presumption reasoning in Janakiramaraju v. Appalaswami and disapproved Narayanaswami Nayadu v. Subramaniyan. It concluded that the Explanation created no presumption either way.

predicates.inam_estate_classification_case: A court is deciding whether land covered by an inam grant constitutes an estate.
predicates.grant_expressed_as_named_village: The grant described the subject of the inam as a village by name.

issues.definition: In an inam estate classification, a grant expressed as one of a named village does not, by itself, produce a presumption that the land is an estate.

issues.legal_issue: A person seeking a declaration that inam land is not an estate bears the burden of proving that it is not an estate and fails if the necessary facts are left unproved.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration that the lands covered by the principal title deed were not an estate.
The grant was of a named village, and minor inams covered some lands within the village.
The dates of the minor inam grants were not established, and the plaintiff did not prove that they postdated the grant of the rest of the village as a named village.
issues.conclusion: The burden rested on the plaintiff to prove that the lands were not an estate, including by showing that the minor inams were granted after the named-village grant. The plaintiff failed to discharge that burden, so the suit was rightly dismissed and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 101, 102 and 103 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a person seeking judgment on asserted facts must prove them; the burden lies on the person who would fail if neither side produced evidence, and the burden as to a particular fact lies on the person asking the court to believe it unless law provides otherwise. Because the legislature created no presumption either way, the plaintiff had to prove the lands were not an estate. District Board, Tanjore v. Noor Mohammad was distinguished because the burden point there rested on counsel's concession and was not decided after discussion.
